Leading them to a place that produces something is more practical than extinguishing them: writing, painting, making crafts, teaching people, or running a small trade are all better than spending them away. From middle age, try things that require a little patience; meditation, yoga and long walks are all fine, and the key is to let yourself know that “I can stop”. When something is pressed down inside, find someone to talk to in time, keep your routine steady, and have a routine check-up once a year.

Advice: do not fight your own desires head-on; restraining them is more practical than extinguishing them. Give that flow of energy a proper outlet: writing, making works, or running a small trade are all better than spending it on drink and gambling. From middle age, try things that require a little patience; light intermittent fasting, giving up alcohol, long-distance running and meditation are all fine, and the key is to let yourself know that “I can stop”. Each month set aside a day or two with no socializing, no drinking, and no scrolling on your phone.

Advice: when you make a large investment elsewhere, first have a local expert assess it. The lawyers and accountants you know are not familiar with the rules in other places, and this consulting fee should not be saved on. When signing a contract, read every clause, especially the payment schedule and the withdrawal terms. Do not touch financial products in unfamiliar fields; what trips you up most easily is what you do not understand yourself.

Advice: deliberately soften your tone. Before stating an opinion, say a sentence of acknowledgment, so that with the same words the other person does not feel pushed by you. When making an important decision, do not rely on a single burst of momentum; let a night pass before settling it, since your failures mostly come from overconfidence and too little deliberation. With family, do not just bury yourself in work; each week ask them privately how they are living.

Advice: open a separate account of your own. As soon as pay comes in, automatically move a sum into it: half to buy things that make you happy and half locked away untouched, which is much more effective than gritting your teeth to save. Invest by the steady road, buying a little at regular intervals in a fixed amount, and do not touch what you do not understand. Even if you do not manage the money at home, you must be able to understand the books, and at least once a year work out the family finances clearly. What truly raises your income is reputation: do a job so well that people actively recommend you.

Advice: when you go elsewhere, do not go empty-handed. Work lined up in advance, a place to live already viewed, and two or three people you know who can put in a word; with these three things, you will be steady however far you go. On arriving in a new place, take the initiative to enter circles, whether a colleague group or an interest-based organization, since your chances all come from people. Keeping a fixed rhythm of contact with family, for example one call a week, is far more useful than calling only when you miss home.

Advice: partner only with people who value contracts and keep the rules. Do not tie up shares with the kind of person for whom “being loyal is enough”. Before cooperating, settle the rules for parting: how the accounts are split, who has the final word, what happens if someone wants to withdraw; how you part matters more than how you start. As for acting as guarantor for others, try not to get involved, because the one who suffers the loss is mostly you.

Advice: eat meals on time and in the right amount, chewing carefully and swallowing slowly. Eat less raw and cold food, less spicy food, and take a walk after eating. When emotions are suppressed for long, the body's rhythm is thrown into disorder too, so when something is on your mind, find someone to talk to early and do not carry it alone. If you plan to get pregnant, do a pre-pregnancy check beforehand, and during pregnancy follow the doctor's arrangements. Have a full health check-up once a year; if your body is not right, see a doctor in time and follow the doctor's words.

Advice: before going into a partnership, say the hard-to-hear things first. Who puts in the money, who decides, how profits are split, and how to withdraw if someone wants out; write it all down in words. It is not that you do not trust each other, but that you leave each other a way out. When dealing with siblings, you are both tough, so do not let either decide for the other, and when something comes up, first ask “how do you want to do it”. At holidays, take the initiative to send a message or arrange a meal; affection comes from keeping up visits, and without visits it fades.

Advice: before going into a partnership, say things clearly. Write each clause of the contract plainly, keep the books open, and check them regularly. What you fear has never been speaking out straight, but holding your words in. Look for partners in fields such as law, education and training, and media, where relying on expertise and the gift of speech suits your rhythm best. When dealing with siblings, argue less over right and wrong and ask one more time what the other thinks; sharing a few meals together in a year is more useful than winning one argument.

Advice: before going into a partnership, say beforehand what needs to be said. How much money is put in, who handles what, how profits are split; write it all into the contract. Most important is that the direction is set by you and that you look over the clauses yourself, and do not be the kind of person who signs whatever others hand over. When siblings or partners ask to borrow money or ask you to act as guarantor, first say “let me go home and think about it”, and answer after a night has passed.

Advice: when you go into a partnership, observe for three to six months first. Get the other party's rhythm clearly before you set about changing things, and before changing, say clearly why you are changing and how. Capital contribution, division of duties and withdrawal should be written down in black and white. With them, you do not need to force closeness; fulfilling the courtesies where needed is enough, and save your energy for people who truly suit you.

Advice: before going into a partnership, openly say the line “if it does not work out, we dissolve”. Capital contribution, division of duties and withdrawal should be written down in black and white. You are not naturally good at long-term ties, and leaving a way out beforehand is steadier than forcing yourself to hold on. With siblings, you do not need to force frequent contact; a call at holidays and truly stepping up when the family has trouble is more effective than surface closeness.

Advice: when your career goes smoothly, separate out money early. Keep an account that only takes money in and never out; as soon as your pay arrives, set a portion aside, and do not wait for spare money before saving. For large spending, give yourself a 24-hour cooling-off period. Invest in fields you are familiar with, do not scatter blindly, and when prices are at a peak, do not add more capital.

Advice: start working on it right away in the years from twenty-five to thirty. Turn fame into something you can keep: a solid qualification, an irreplaceable set of skills, or a brand of your own. After choosing a direction, work at it for at least five to seven years before discussing a change of career. Do not lock yourself only into the road of “relying on charm” either; hard positions such as manager, team leader and business lead are things you can do too. If you plan to have a child, put postpartum recovery and emotional swings into the plan beforehand.

Advice: learn to show weakness in front of those close to you. When tired, say you are tired, and when you do not know, say you do not know; this does not cost you value, and is in fact the door through which people come close to you. When choosing a partner, look for someone a little more experienced than you, so that you are willing to lower your guard; when living together, change giving advice into asking “what do you think”. At work, follow directions that help people such as law, medicine, education and public welfare, where you work with more devotion than anyone. Do not cut your standards flat with one stroke; leave the people beside you a little room to be imperfect.

Advice: try showing weakness in front of him once. On one small matter, say “I can't manage this, you do it”. When he has a chance to take care of you, the relationship will not be one-sided. Give less advice and ask more “what do you think”, even if you have long had the answer in your heart. If he does not do it as well as you, allow him to be a little slower and a little wrong. When you are dissatisfied inside, do not suppress it; say it the same day, since whenever you suppress it you turn cold-faced, and that hurts more than a quarrel.

Advice: in front of your son, step back half a pace. For what he can decide himself, let him decide, and if he gets it wrong, look back over it together, and do not rush to decide for him. Be willing to invest in education, especially for a son; over the long run this is well worth it, and in old age you can mostly count on him. From small, help your child build some ability to bear pressure, and also teach him to speak properly in front of others.

Advice: in other places, speak more discreetly than at home. The same blunt sentence may be taken by people elsewhere as provocation. After marrying far away, do not be the go-between for the two sides; you see the conflicts in the family clearly, but once you step in to mediate, both sides will suspect you. For contracts and guarantees you are not sure about, set them aside for now and have someone look them over before signing. On arriving in a new place, first get to know one or two local friends and ask clearly about the rules of the place, which saves far more trouble than groping about alone.

Advice: in other places, speak more discreetly than at home. The same blunt sentence, which locals know how to take from you, may be taken by people elsewhere as provocation. During business trips and long journeys, do not rush to sign contracts and do not easily act as guarantor for others; documents you are not sure about should be taken home and signed only after someone has looked them over. On arriving in a new place, first get to know one or two locals and ask clearly about the rules of the place, which saves far more trouble than groping about on your own.

Advice: when talking within the clan, change how you open first. Change “you are wrong to do that” into “this is what I think”, and the sting is very different. When the other person is complaining, listen to everything first and do not rush to offer solutions. For partnerships, choose reasonable people, and do not let sisterly feeling replace a contract; write the clauses that need writing one by one clearly, and check the books regularly. For matters that truly must be argued, wait until a private moment, since at the dining table there is no arguing over who wins.

Advice: in major family matters, say your thoughts in full at least once. Whether the other person listens after that is their business, but you cannot have not said it even once. When you pool money with others for trade or business, how much money goes in, who manages which part, and how the accounts are split should be written clearly from the start; do not fear hurting feelings, since saying the hard-to-hear words first means you stay together longer. Make cooperation short-term, and settle the account once each task is done. Do not take on all matters of emotion; before helping, ask yourself whether you have the time.

Advice: at work, take roads that require you to make up your own mind. Starting a business, sales and specialized technical work are all fine; do not force yourself into a frame of the old order. In love there is no need to race against time; once you can stand firm by yourself, the person you meet will be able to hold you up. You do not need to learn to act coy, but you can learn to accept the umbrella that others hand you: when someone cares about you, say thank you and accept it, because you have been sheltering yourself for too long.

Advice: before marriage, get yourself a small home as a backup card. After marriage, you and your husband buy the one meant for long-term living, while the small one keeps its ownership under your own name. When deciding to buy a big house, first have a legal professional look over the contract, and check ownership, mortgage and handover time clause by clause. Choose decoration by the standard of not going out of date in ten years; solid wood furniture, and classic styles whether Chinese or European, all suit you. Keep a little ritual of holidays at home, put up a wall of family photos, and keep a few old things; that is your dose of reassurance.

My advice: in your career, actively seize cross-city and cross-region opportunities. Every change of environment broadens your knowledge, so do not wait for the company to arrange it; ask for projects and postings elsewhere yourself. Each year, spend at least a few days in a city you have never visited, meet two or three people from different industries, and write down what you hear. Before a long trip, settle the itinerary, the lodging and a backup plan in advance; do not wait until you arrive to work it out, because you cannot stand sudden disorder.

My advice: in your work position, build up your ability to execute and to manage money. Whether to start your own business depends on whether the Wealth palace has Prosperity and Power, not on a Martial star in the Career palace alone. The thing to guard against most is being domineering: before an important decision, make it a rule to find one or two people to voice opposing views, and decide only after hearing them. Add a word of recognition for colleagues and subordinates, and only then can the team be led. The people who can help you are mostly in the area of capital and resources, so investors and elders who run real businesses are worth more of your time. With Martial transforming to Prosperity in the Career palace, this Prosperity may only refer to money within the position that you manage and hold in your hands, which does not mean the money belongs to you.

My advice: in your work position, build up your ability to execute and to manage money. Whether to start your own business depends on whether the Wealth palace has Prosperity and Power, not on a Martial star in the Career palace alone. The thing to guard against most is being domineering: before an important decision, make it a rule to find one or two people to voice opposing views, and decide only after hearing them. Add a word of recognition for colleagues and subordinates, and only then can the team be led. The people who can help you are mostly in the area of capital and resources, so investors and elders who run real businesses are worth more of your time.

My advice: when you earn a lot, set money aside first. Move a fixed amount into an account that is not easy to touch, and spend only what remains. For large expenses, set yourself a rule: above a certain amount, wait three days before deciding. Do not touch high-risk things you do not understand; putting your money into the field you are good at is more realistic. For anything involving money, put it in writing in black and white, which can save you a great deal of trouble later.

My advice: keep a boundary in front of your elders. Respect does not mean flattery, and caring does not mean sacrifice. If there is something you do not want to do, say so gently and clearly; that is far better than swallowing it, doing it and then feeling wronged. For matters with your parents-in-law, let your husband speak up, and do not shoulder them stubbornly on your own. From the age of forty-five, take the initiative to arrange a health check-up for both of them once a year, and if a problem turns up, follow the doctor's advice. If your parents often quarrel, it is mostly just quarrelling, the affection is still there, and there is no need to worry too much.

My advice: cultivate something that belongs only to you. Yoga, reading, baking or growing flowers are all fine, provided you do not need anyone to join you and you enjoy doing it. Its use is that when you are alone your heart still feels full, instead of waiting for someone to come and fill it. When you feel anxious inside, tell the other person directly; once asked, the matter usually dissolves, so do not stage a play alone in your heart. Set aside a stretch of time each week when no one disturbs you, rain or shine.

My advice: after marriage, keep an account of your own. Keep it separate from the family's joint account; this is not a matter of distrusting the other person, but of your nature needing this support. Choose steady investments: a home to live in and a property to rent out, or a project whose returns you can see clearly, and do not touch high-risk speculation. Do not be overly frugal either; for what is worth spending on yourself, do not cut corners.

My advice: learn to keep things simple. To refuse, no explanation is needed; “it is not convenient for me right now” is enough, and do not add reasons after saying it. When lending money, set yourself a ceiling, and beyond it say plainly that you have none. When you are with someone of the opposite sex, make your limits clear from the start; where it needs saying, do not be vague, which takes less energy than clearing up misunderstandings later. Who is a true friend and who only remembers you when they need something becomes clear after a few months; once you have judged, simply see them less and less, with no need to fall out.

My advice: learn to say one honest sentence: I cannot help with this, you have to go through it yourself once. It is not cold-hearted; some people have to fall once before they are willing to stand up. Choosing work that helps people suits you best: civil service, teaching, medicine and culture all fit your nature; the business world need not be avoided either, except that you prefer to rely on real ability rather than on a glib tongue. Besides that, set aside two hours each week with no phone calls and no worrying about other people's affairs; that is where you recover your strength.

My advice: learn to say one sentence: “I can't do it this time.” Refusing is not unfilial; it leaves a path open for yourself. For family matters such as contributing money, contributing effort and caring for the elderly, put them on the table early and divide them per head; do not assume that whoever is free does it, because the one who is free will always be you. If you really go into business together with your siblings, affection is affection and accounts are accounts: how much each puts in, who manages what and how it is divided, write it down and sign it, which is better than falling out later.

My advice: practise saying no. This is not coldness, but a way of saving a little strength for yourself; only when you stand firm yourself can you help others. On money matters, say the unwelcome words first: how much is borrowed and when it will be repaid, written out clearly; if you really do business together, sign the contract and hand the books to a more practical person to manage. Before agreeing to help, ask yourself one question: once I finish this, will the next month be more tiring? If so, say plainly that this time you cannot.

My advice: when you assign work, add one sentence on why. When others can keep up, the friction is cut by half. With your partner and your family, make your care visible: picking them up once or remembering a day matters more than leaving it unspoken. From middle age your friends will become fewer but deeper; do not despise the small number, and hold on tight to those few. In the evening, give yourself a corner where you can take off your armour; this is not becoming soft, but a way to catch your breath.

My advice: have regular health check-ups. The “Complete Book”, volume two, under the Health palace, the Seven Killings entry, says “Seven Killings brings many misfortunes in childhood and often hemorrhoids in adulthood”; when you are examined, do not skip the anus and rectum items. If your body feels unwell, see a doctor early and follow the doctor's advice; do not bear it on your own. Eat less spicy food, cut down on tobacco and alcohol, and eat more vegetables. It is good that you like exercise, but you need to add some stretching and flexibility work; do not train only heavily, and do not push on while injured. The hardest lesson, and also the most important, is learning how to rest.

My advice: to every invitation promising “quick money” or a “life change overnight”, refuse outright. No reason needs to be given. When friends want to borrow money or want you to sign as guarantor, say you will think it over and answer a day later. Keep people not through liveliness but through what you have genuinely accomplished: holding on firmly to two or three people you can work with is far better than knowing a hundred.

My advice: for everyone you want to cooperate with openly, make inquiries first. Look at their past reputation; this is not being calculating, because once you are dragged into other people's scandals, you suffer the greatest loss. Keep up long-term contact with friends of high standing and upright conduct, and do not look for them only when something comes up. With those of poor reputation, fade out early, and do not wait until trouble happens before washing your hands of them. Whoever asks to borrow money or asks you to sign as guarantor, first think about whether the matter could be brought into the light; if not, refuse outright.

My advice: with a friend you truly care about, empathise first and analyse afterwards. When she pours out her troubles, what she needs is to be understood, not to have them solved; first say “if it were me, I would be upset too”, and then discuss what to do. Do not treat friends as a case study; a relationship needs a little warmth that does not argue reason. With people you truly care about, learn to give way a step: it is not losing, but leaving the relationship a way to survive. Your male friends are not many, but they are usually the kind who are truly there when something happens, and they are worth maintaining well.

My advice: with people you truly care about, learn to give way a step. It is not losing, but leaving this relationship a way to survive. When friends pour out their troubles, listen to the end first and take in their feelings first; do not rush to analyse who is right or wrong. At the drinking table, drink two glasses less, because a sentence you say after drinking is the one most likely to cause trouble. Keep business partnerships separate from friendship, and sign what needs to be signed. You yourself keep the rules; what to guard against is befriending the wrong people, not that you will cause trouble yourself.

My advice: with your elders, keep in regular contact and argue less. One call a week, even if only five minutes, works better than a long talk once every six months. Do not keep thinking about persuading them; what they need is to be held in your heart, not to be argued down. For your parents' affairs, first ask how they want to handle it, and then offer advice. It is the same with superiors: stating your judgement clearly is enough, and do not contend with them inwardly.

My advice: be careful not to let praise bind you. Wanting to be a good daughter-in-law is not wrong, but do not trade your boundaries for a compliment. For matters of the elderly and the household, put the division of tasks on the table early and discuss it per head; do not assume that whoever is handy does it. For what elders have promised, and for the elders' property and contracts, write it down in black and white while everyone is still clear-headed, and do not count on a verbal agreement settling it. When your parents are getting on in years, take them for check-ups regularly, and do not wait until something happens before rushing to the hospital.

My advice: use a lecturing tone less. When something comes up, listen to her fully first, and then give your view. The old books say that with Heavenly Beam in the Spouse palace, the wife should be older than you; a wife several years older than you is not a problem, so do not let the age gap become a reason for you to hesitate. In love it is fine to be a little slow, but do not trap yourself with a list of demands; once character and attitude are right, take one step further. When the two of you are tense, speak it out; the coldness of your cool handling hurts more than an argument.

My advice: confront others less, and do not swallow your anger either. After a quarrel, find someone to talk to or write it out on the same day; only when your energy flows smoothly will your body relax along with it. Eat meals on time and in the right amount, chew thoroughly and swallow slowly, cut down on raw, cold and spicy food, and do not overeat. Have a full health check-up once a year, and after forty check more often; when something in your body is not right, see a doctor promptly and follow the doctor's advice.

My advice: choose one or two things early and go deep. Turn the opportunities brought by your looks and your affinity with people into a trade that can support you for life, or a brand of your own. Art, entertainment, beauty and other trades that deal with people all suit you, but do not walk on one leg only, namely charm. In love, set yourself a screening standard, for example only discussing settling down after knowing someone a full six months. With money, leave a sum untouched; liveliness is liveliness, but the books must have a foundation.

My advice: buy yourself a small home early. Even if it is small, it is a real support. When signing a contract, read it word by word before signing; the floor area, the handover date and the compensation for breach are the few points to look at especially carefully, and if you do not understand, pay for someone to look it over. Before construction starts, let the neighbours know, which can avoid most of the trouble. When choosing a home, try to choose a place that is bright and airy; the decoration can be bold and have personality, but do not make it both dark and heavy, because over time your mood will be the first to be unable to bear it.

My advice: in daily life, train yourself to decide faster. For small matters, limit yourself to one minute and then settle; once that is well practised, you will dare to speak up on big matters. For an important report or a salary discussion, write out your words beforehand and read them through twice; do not wait until you get there to think. Do not rush to start your own company; first, on a good foundation, choose exactly one direction to go deep in and build a reputation; if you really want to be independent, find a partner who knows practical work. If you plan to have a child, before the birth discuss with your team how you will return and how you will stay in contact, and do not leave yourself at home completely out of touch.

My advice: open an account that is a hassle to withdraw from. Each month, move three-tenths of your income into it first, and the rest is what you may spend. Set a ceiling on a few big categories: for clothing, beauty and travel, write down how much each may take in a year, and check against it. For investing, choose short cycles and connections your own reach can verify; for a project introduced by word of mouth within your circle, investigate the contract and background thoroughly before putting money in. For the household accounts, I suggest that each person manages a part and records it separately.

My advice: open an account that belongs only to you. Each month, as soon as your salary arrives, automatically transfer two-tenths into it, to be spent only on yourself. However solid your relationship is, build up an independent savings fund of at least one year of living costs; this is not to guard against anyone, but to give you something to lean on. Manage money the steady way: term deposits, stable funds and insurance, putting capital preservation first and avoiding high-risk speculation. For gifts and favours between people, set an annual ceiling, and when it is exceeded say plainly that the budget is used up. If your pay is lower than your worth, take the initiative to negotiate.

My advice: when investing elsewhere, first choose a city you know well. Before investing, have a local expert assess it, and read the contract clause by clause, especially the payment schedule and the exit terms. A high-return project introduced by an acquaintance is the thing most likely to lower your guard; the closer the acquaintance, the more clearly you must ask.

My advice, as a father: actively accept your child's “headstrong” nature. Do not try to lock your child into a gentle, obedient mould, which will crush the child's natural gifts. Set few rules, and once set, hold to them; for the rest, let go and let your child learn by bumping into things. When your child talks back, hear it all before you speak; the more you press, the more your child will resist.

My advice: head toward positions in start-ups, the arts, media and reform-minded work. These are all places that can contain this breakthrough energy of yours, so do not force yourself to stay in a traditional unit where everything follows set rules. In love, settle down a little later; when young you are too impulsive, and the people you meet come and go without pattern, so wait until you have settled before choosing. In youth you broke down many old things; by middle age you should try building once, not rebuilding the past but building something new that belongs only to you, choosing one direction and seeing it through for a full five years.

My advice: stay and work in a stable unit. Do not easily go out on your own to start a business; if you really want to go into partnership, find a partner with drive who can push you to run. Each time you finish a task, take the initiative to tell your superior clearly which part was yours, and do not count on others to record the credit for you. Each year, set one goal you have to stretch to reach; if you stay too long in a position that is too comfortable, more than three years, you should move.

My advice: before starting a family, live independently elsewhere for a year or two. Strive to claim this stretch of time for yourself, and you will be able to use it forever afterwards. After starting a family you will travel less, and you can lean toward remote work or a two-place arrangement; you do not need to put down roots in one place to feel at ease. Before a long trip, settle the itinerary, the lodging and the return plan in advance, and let your family know. If you feel stifled on the road, call a friend and talk it out, and do not hold it in alone and brood ever deeper.

My advice: train “let me think about it” into a habit of speech. When someone has just asked you for help, do not agree on the spot; answer after a night. For anything involving money and signatures, say “this is not convenient for me”, with no need to explain much. To widen your circle, start from professional channels: trade associations, gatherings of colleagues and classes. The people you meet in these places walk the same path as you and are more trustworthy than acquaintances at a drinking table.

My advice: change “what I say goes” into “I hear what you say”. The older your child grows, the more your child will respond to this approach, and talking things through works better than tight control. Each week set aside a stretch of time that belongs only to you and your child, with no talk of results and no talk of plans, just playing together. The words “Mom loves you” are spoken especially rarely in your home, and are worth the effort of saying a few more times.

My advice: treat your career as the main line and just do it with ease; this is your most solid support. In love, do not set standards too rigid; whether your rhythms match matters more than whether the conditions look good, and when you meet someone who can run forward with you, give yourself some time to try it slowly. When you talk, add a word of recognition, and your firmness will prick people less. Leave a crack open for those close to you as well, so that they know you also need someone to love you.

My advice: treat your career as the main axis of your life. This is a clear-headed choice, not a step back. When looking for a partner, do not look only at conditions; look for someone you sincerely admire in some respect, and who can also hold your independence; if they cannot hold it, however outstanding they are, they are not suited to you. At the same time, learn to accept your soft side: when tired you may say you are tired, and you may receive the goodwill others offer; do not treat loneliness as the price of being strong.

My advice: separate family affection from money when you count. Affection may be close, but for a loan write a receipt, and for a partnership sign a contract; who puts in how much and how it is divided should be made clear from the start. As for acting as a guarantor, say plainly that you will not, with no need to explain. If you really want to work together, choose directions such as food and drink, leisure and entertainment, services or the arts, which suit you all better than trades that compete on hard physical effort.

My advice: first stabilise your daily life. Cut down on alcohol and late-night eating, eat until seven-tenths full, and eat more vegetables. You have a gift for exercise; running, swimming and ball games all work, and using up your spare energy is better than suppressing it. Have a health check-up once a year, and for the routine screenings for women, follow them by age; if you feel unwell, see a doctor promptly and follow the doctor's advice, and do not drag it out and then search online for answers. If you plan to become pregnant, give up alcohol, coffee and late nights early; during pregnancy, do not starve yourself or train too hard for the sake of your figure.

My advice: fix your daily routine. Try to go to bed at the same hour and get up at the same hour every day, which is more effective than any tonic food. Eat a little lighter, go easy on spice and caffeine, and do not drink coffee after the afternoon. Choose exercise with a rhythm: brisk walking, light jogging, swimming or cycling, three times a week for half an hour each, so that the body leads the mind to cool down. Have a routine check-up once a year, and let the doctor arrange which items to check; if you feel unwell inside, do not look up symptoms online and frighten yourself, but see a doctor and follow the doctor's advice.

My advice: fix your daily routine. Sleeping and eating times matter more than what you eat. Have regular health check-ups every year, and keep your own record of your menstrual cycles; if they are irregular for several months in a row, see a doctor and follow the doctor's advice, and do not drag it out. If you want a child, first keep a stable rhythm of life for half a year to a year and then decide; during pregnancy, ask your family to help you keep track of the prenatal check-up schedule, and do not skip it because of a business trip. As you approach perimenopause, you can see a doctor early to discuss how to look after yourself; the physical discomfort of your type is usually more pronounced than in others.

My advice: when others agree to something by word of mouth, first discount it a little in your mind. See whether what they agreed to last time was actually done, and then decide how much to trust. Two or three close confidants are enough; put your effort into the long term. When you are with friends of the opposite sex, put the boundaries in the open: meet alone less, do not get into the other person's family matters, and do not pour out all your own private matters either. Do not mention important matters that are not yet settled in front of ordinary friends.

My advice: gather your energy into one or two things. Set a time limit, for example, stay with one direction for a full five years before discussing a change. Do not settle important decisions when your emotions are running high; sleep on it and decide the next day. For spending and love, set a ceiling for yourself, and stop when it is exceeded. Among friends, choose three or five you can truly talk with and befriend deeply, and keeping up contact with the rest is enough. Your period of breakthrough comes in middle age, and only then do the connections and skills you have accumulated truly pay off.

My advice: yield the credit on the surface to your leader. Keep the reputation for yourself: outwardly, let him have face, and inwardly, let people know that you were the one who got the job done. It is the same with your father: argue less about right and wrong, ask more about how he has been lately, pay special attention to his heart, eyes and blood pressure, and after fifty urge him to have regular check-ups.

My advice: hand the saving of money over to a mechanism, and do not rely on willpower. As soon as your salary arrives in the account, have a sum transferred away automatically, and spend what remains freely. Invest the steady way, buying a fixed amount regularly, and do not touch high-risk things you do not understand. Think clearly about which of your skills you could develop to the point where people introduce clients to you on their own, and put your time there. One more point: if your love life is in disorder, your spending will fall into disorder too, so while a relationship is not yet steady, do not make large decisions.

My advice: make regular health check-ups a fixed habit. Have a full check-up once a year, and if something is wrong with your body, see a doctor immediately and follow the doctor's advice; do not bear it on your own. For exercise, do both aerobic work and strength training, building muscle and stamina firmly, but be sure to pay attention to safety, and do not rely on strength to lift weights that are too heavy. Go easy on tobacco, alcohol and overly spicy food.

My advice: for the details that keep replaying in your heart, find a place to let them out. Write them down, draw them, or go out for a walk alone, and do not let them clog your chest and become inner drain. When you are with other people, first set a clear distance and sense of proportion, which spares you a great deal of trouble. Go in the directions of art, design, law and psychological counselling, which value expertise and can also hold complex emotions; your sensitivity is a strength, not a flaw. When your emotions surge, do not decide in haste; wait a day and then speak.

My advice: say plainly what you want. When tired, say you are tired, and when you want a hug, say so, because other people cannot read minds. Hardness and softness can exist together: by day you are still the one who shines, and in the evening allow yourself to need someone to comfort you too. When the Sun is Fallen (weak), your temper becomes even more headstrong, and once you have made up your mind you refuse to turn back, easily hurting people when you argue your point; train the habit of counting three seconds before the words leave your mouth, and use your eloquence to get things done, not to fight over winning and losing.

My advice: practise affection the way you practise action. One hug a day, one stretch of time each week spent only with your child with no talk of results, and a birthday properly celebrated once. Change “I arrange” into “let us discuss”; the older your child grows, the more your child will respond to this approach, and conflicts will shrink considerably.

My advice: write down your criteria for choosing a partner. Separate which points are your final limit and which you can yield on; black and white is more reliable than how you feel at the moment. Do not rush to settle; get to know someone for more than half a year before discussing marriage, and marrying a little later is mostly a good thing for you. Your future husband is probably also a person with talent, good at dealing with people and quite charming, but since you both enjoy liveliness, someone has to take the initiative to keep stability in your life. If you meet someone who drags things out without being clear, cut it off cleanly and early.

My advice: put your greatest effort into two things. Build a reputation and avoid disputes; when these two are done well, your financial fortune will naturally be steady. For investing, choose directions you have studied and understood; copyright, intellectual property, education and other fields that live on information suit you best, so do not chase the crowd. Set yourself a few criteria for judgement, act when they are met, and do not keep researching until the opportunity runs away. Costs such as settlement money and lawyers' fees are the most unjust to pay, so for important matters put the wording in writing first.

My advice: put your best energy into one main source of income. Do not attack on all fronts. Two or three investment directions are enough; set aside new things you do not understand, and keep enough cash in hand before discussing anything else. If you want to try a new project, set a ceiling first: invest only what you can afford to lose. On payday each month, automatically transfer a sum into an account that is not easy to touch; do not rely on self-discipline, rely on automatic deduction.

My advice: save your sharpest words for work. At home, change the way you speak: first say what you understand, and then say what you disagree with. When the urge to win rises, remind yourself that what you truly need is not to win, but for the other person to be willing to hear you out. Law, consulting, research and psychology, trades that live on penetrating insight, suit you best, and going in these directions puts your gift in the right place. When suspicion arises, ask one direct question, which beats a week of guessing on your own.

My advice: divide your friends into three tiers and treat them accordingly. For ordinary friends, try to make many and use them to hear news; for close confidants, choose two or three and put your effort into the long term; for important matters not yet settled, do not mention a single word in front of others. When judging someone, do not listen to what they say; look at whether what they agreed to with you last time was done. Before cooperating, bring the division of work and the split of the accounts into the open, however good the relationship.

My advice: divide your friends clearly into three tiers. They are those who give you a hand in your career, those you can do business with, and those who are only good for eating and drinking together; once this is clear in your mind, you will not count on the wrong people. When employing people, give small tasks first, and add burden only after they succeed; do not hand over both the money and the seal at the start. Loyalty among brothers is where you most easily stumble: for guarantees, loans and partnerships, wait a day before answering before you agree to any of these three.

My advice: make a yearly routine check-up a fixed habit. Do not skip the full check-up or the routine items for women, and if something is wrong with your body, see a doctor immediately and follow the doctor's advice. While preparing for pregnancy, running nonstop while suppressing your emotions makes the body likely to refuse to cooperate; reducing pressure is more effective than pushing hard. For exercise, do both aerobic work and strength training, and pay attention to safety without relying on brute strength.

My advice: write your boundaries down in advance. Which matters you will not help with, which words must not be said to you, and how much time and money each month are kept for yourself alone. Decide ahead of time and follow it when the time comes; do not wait until someone speaks up and then decide on the spot, because by then you will most likely soften. If a relationship leaves you more tired the longer you stay in it, set aside a day to think about it seriously: is it just this period, or is it always like this? If you really cannot make up your mind, find a friend who is not involved and tell the whole story from beginning to end, and you will hear it yourself.

My advice: change supervising into setting rules. State your final limit clearly, let go of the details, and let your child bear the consequences of a wrong choice. With a daughter, give fewer orders and discuss more, talking with her as a person who can decide for herself. Do not give up your whole career for your child; you have a sky of your own, and between mother and child that actually makes things more comfortable. When your child grows up and goes to develop elsewhere, call on a fixed schedule and remember what is going on in her life, and distance will not stretch the bond.

My advice: push marriage back a little. First look at character and the foundation for living together, and do not let feeling alone lead you. When you quarrel, the problem cannot be solved that same day; wait until the anger has gone down before discussing it, which works especially well for the two of you. Your charm comes from talent and bearing, but whether the relationship lasts depends on whether you are willing to say what is in your heart: regularly having a serious talk with her is more useful than giving her anything.

My advice: put your professional boundaries in the open. Have fewer private social engagements, and discuss business in public places where possible, which can avoid most of the trouble. Do not bring emotions into working relationships, and for hard words wait a day before saying them. If you plan to have a child, it is best to wait until you hold a stable stretch of career in your hands before arranging it, and do not crowd it into the two years when you most need to advance. Do not mix your ledger of personal favours into your professional credibility; this is what you most need to hold firm.

My advice: turn keeping in touch into a fixed habit. One call a week and a few visits home each year, going by the calendar rather than by mood. For your elders' health, just do routine check-ups as a matter of course, and if there is a problem listen to the doctor; do not frighten yourself by relying on the chart. It is the same at the office: you and your superior can read each other easily, and you see through him without saying, while he also feels examined by you; if you have a thought, say it directly, and do not treat an air of mystery as a protective charm.

My advice: take the initiative to speak up about what you have done. This is not boasting of credit, but letting people know who did the work. In a meeting, state your own judgement first, and do not ask others what they think as soon as you walk in; if you keep asking, you will lose your own view as well. When a new task outside the usual rules comes up, find someone who dares to charge ahead to team up with; you take care of steadiness and he takes care of the charge. Let go of what should be let go, and do not treat stubbornness as responsibility.

My advice: see yourself as the one who supplies resources. Do not be the one who draws the road: give tuition, opportunities and knowledge as best you can, and let your child choose which road to take. Manage principles, not details; honesty, safety and attitude toward people should be managed to the end, while what to wear and which subject's homework comes first should be let go. When your child does wrong, do not rush to lecture; let your child bear all the consequences, and then ask one question: what do you plan to do next time?

My advice: save the words that need to be made clear for a private moment. Contradicting someone right in front of others wins you face but loses the relationship. When talking with your parents, ask more and comment less; even if the reasoning they give is out of date, listen to all of it first. Suppressing it is not as good as choosing a quiet moment to say it once and be done, and once said, turn the page. At work, by contrast, you suit a superior who dares to speak plainly; you can understand the meaning behind their harsh words, so do not be frightened by the tone on the surface.

My advice: say it in words. You are used to suppressing things and expect her to see it for herself, but she mostly does not; for something in your heart that you cannot get past, saying it clearly that same day is far better than suppressing it for a week. When choosing a partner, do not look only at conditions; see whether her emotions can stay steady. Before and after marriage, settle properly how to get along with your mother and with your wife: who decides big matters, how near to live to each other and how to arrange the New Year holiday; if this is made clear early, most of the awkwardness later can be avoided.

My advice: spend your energy on speaking only for things that are truly important. When you want to talk back, pause for three seconds first and ask yourself what will change once you have said it. Do not wait to think a decision through completely; act when the information reaches seven or eight tenths, and set yourself a deadline. Trust can be given step by step: try it first on small things, then add more according to the results, which works better than standing by and watching for half a year. When you feel stifled inside, find someone who will hear you out; you are the kind of person who can let go only after saying it clearly.

My advice: put the focus of your earning on turning yourself into a brand. The louder your reputation, the higher your income. For spending, draw a line yourself: set a monthly ceiling on spending for your image, and when it is exceeded wait until next month. Most important, before marriage make clear how money will be counted: each person keeps an independent account and shared expenses are split in an agreed way, because a person like you will not live comfortably once someone else controls you financially.

My advice: treat going out into the world as your proper path. Relying on a refined skill or a specialty to build a reputation is much stronger than staying put in one place. While exploring freely, set yourself a time limit, for example three years, to dig deep into one field so that your talent has somewhere to take root. When looking for a partner, look for someone who can accept your constant change, not someone who wants to keep you under tight control.

My advice: turn keeping in touch with your parents into a fixed habit. One call a week and one trip home a month is far better than living together and quarrelling every day; your relationship is one that gets along well only with a bit of distance. Where views do not match, do not argue; listening without following is enough. From the age of forty-five, take the initiative to help your parents arrange a health check-up every year, go with them, and carry out the results as the doctor advises. At work you suit a flexible superior; with a rigid leader, argue less and deliver more results.

My advice: turn keeping in touch with your parents into a fixed habit. One call a week and one trip home a month is far better than living together and quarrelling every day; this bond depends on a bit of distance to last. Where views do not match, do not argue; listening without following is enough. From the age of forty-five, take the initiative to help them arrange a health check-up every year, go with them, and carry out the results as the doctor advises. When you are with your parents-in-law, pull back on your social side; there is no need to pretend to be someone else, and show less of that eye-catching charm in front of them.

My advice: turn exercise into a small fixed thing each day. Walking, swimming or yoga are all fine; the key is to do it every day, not to occasionally train in one fierce burst. Drink enough water, eat fewer sweets and high-energy foods, and keep your meals a little plain. Have a health check-up once a year, and treat blood sugar and weight as the two items to monitor; if the numbers are not right, see a doctor and follow the doctor's advice. When you are unhappy inside, find someone to talk to, and do not hold it alone and get through it by eating.

My advice: turn exercise into a small fixed thing each day. Walking, swimming or yoga are all fine; the key is to do it every day. Keep your meals a little plain, go easy on sweets, white rice and white flour, and drink enough water. If you plan to have a child, before preparing for pregnancy see a doctor for a round of examinations and conditioning; during pregnancy blood sugar must be monitored even more, and prenatal check-ups should follow the doctor's schedule. From the age of forty-five, exercise at least three times a week, do not skip the yearly check-up, and if you feel unwell inside, see a doctor promptly and follow the doctor's advice.

My advice: use your power of choice to pick the right track, not to try everything one by one. Sales and entertainment, any work that depends on reading and handling people, you are good at all of it; do not force yourself to endure a nine-to-five administrative position, because you cannot sit still. Set yourself two rules: do not close deals at the drinking table, and do not sign while your emotions are running high. Middle age is your turning point; if you keep a steady heart and turn the connections you built up in youth into one or two things that truly succeed, the second half will be solid.

My advice: first cut down on alcohol and late-night eating. Eat until seven-tenths full, eat more vegetables, and go easier on oily, spicy and heating food. You have a gift for exercise; putting your spare energy into running, ball games and swimming is far better than suppressing it or spending it on drinking. Have a health check-up once a year, and if you drink a lot in daily life, tell the doctor plainly and do not skip the items that need checking; if you feel unwell, see a doctor promptly and follow the doctor's advice, and do not look for answers online yourself. The two words moderation and restraint are the lifelong lesson for you.

My advice: put the focus on your career. Your professional ability is your voice. The thing to guard against most is being domineering: before an important decision, make it a rule to hear one or two opposing views and then decide. Add a word of recognition for colleagues and subordinates, and only then can the team be led. The people who can help you are mostly in the area of capital and resources, so investors and elders who run real businesses are worth more of your time. With Martial transforming to Prosperity in the Career palace, this Prosperity may only refer to money within the position that you manage and hold in your hands, which does not mean the money belongs to you.

My suggestion: put the focus on your career. Your professional ability is your voice. The thing to guard against most is being domineering: before important decisions, make it a rule to hear one or two opposing views and then decide. Add a word of acknowledgement for colleagues and subordinates, and only then can the team be led. The people who can help you are mostly on the side of capital and resources, so investors and elders who run real businesses are worth keeping up with. As for whether to go into business for yourself, look at whether the Wealth palace has Prosperity.

My suggestion: put the focus on your career. This is not a regret of yours, but the smoothest path. Head toward positions with real authority and hard targets, and do not wear yourself down in a clerical post; if you do start a business, find a meticulous partner who can handle the final steps to make up for what you lack. When managing people, add a word on why, so that people respect you rather than fear you.

My advice: put the focus on your career. Relying on a refined skill or a specialty to build a reputation is your steadiest path. Going out into the world is stronger than staying in one place, and cross-city and cross-industry opportunities are all worth trying. Set yourself a rule: do not change tracks before you have done one thing for a full three years, because accumulation that is not yet deep enough is your greatest risk. If you start a business, find a meticulous partner who seeks stability to make up for your weak points.

My advice: focus on turning yourself into a brand. Be an adviser, the person the industry thinks of first; the louder your reputation, the higher your income. For the financial details, find a professional to help you keep control, add a second layer of confirmation for large expenses, and do not decide alone. Invest the steady way, hold good assets for the long term, and do not touch high-risk quick money. Planning the household money together with your wife is far more effective than you counting the accounts alone.

My advice: divide your money into three parts. Put the largest part somewhere it can be kept for the long term, such as a home to live in, or low-risk deposits and finance, and leave it there in peace; keep a small part for emergencies; and keep another small part solely for trying out opportunities, so that even losing it all does not affect your life. For investing, you suit buying and holding, not frequent in and out, and you should not touch high-risk financial products. Each year, set a fixed budget that you must spend, to be used on health check-ups, learning and rest. Only when your marriage is stable will your wealth be stable.

My advice: turn your sharpness into persuasiveness. Keep the content sharp, but soften the tone, the pace and the expression, so that people are willing to hear you out. Give your opinions in private; in public, talk only about the matter and do not comment on people. If you want to work for yourself, take the road of knowledge services, training, consulting, personal media or legal services, building up clients through your reputation. Having a child does not mean cutting off from work; your communication skills are strong, so keep in touch online during leave and return to a regular meeting rhythm faster than others after the birth, only that under double pressure you must watch your stomach and intestines, and not push on by relying on your body.

My advice: choose the military or police, handicrafts, start-ups, reform and reconstruction. These are all trades where you can break things down and still build them up again; do not go into positions that follow the old sequence, or you will be ground down by boredom. When you have leapfrogging ideas, write them down at once and then fill in the steps in between; do not count on others to keep up. Middle age is a threshold for you: choose one field, truly settle down and work at it for a full five years, which decides whether you are a pioneer for life or only someone who knows how to break things.

My advice: choose a home that is quiet, independent and good for privacy. A private house with a small yard or a suburban area is the first choice, and an apartment in a noisy part of town should rarely be considered. If your circumstances allow, buy yourself a small home early as a backup card; this is not distrust of your other half, but a person like you needs in the heart a way of retreat that belongs only to you. Decorate in a neat and practical direction: little ornament, plenty of storage, and a corner left where no one disturbs you.

My advice: choose a home that is quiet, independent and good for privacy. A private house with a small yard or a suburban area is the first choice, and an apartment in the middle of noisy streets should rarely be considered. Decorate in a neat and practical direction: little ornament, plenty of storage, and a room or a corner that belongs only to you, where you do not have to deal with anyone when you step in. At home, hold few gatherings, and if you want liveliness, arrange to meet outside.

My advice: choose one direction and stay with it for at least five to seven years before discussing a change of trade. If you change too often, you will not build up real ability in your hands. Starting a business is fine, but hand the books to a calm partner to manage, while you only run outside, meet people and expand the market. Your benefactors are mostly the few best-liked people in your circle, and opportunities all come through people. Do not let love affairs drag into your work; this is where you are most likely to overturn the cart.

My advice: change the way you talk with your child. Change “you should” into “we hope”, and change “why did you” into “we feel”. When your child talks back, do not rush to counter; wait until both sides are calm and then discuss. When your child asks why, do not find it annoying, and if you cannot answer, look it up together. In the teenage years, pay even more attention to the weight of your words; one harsh sentence may be remembered by your child for many years.

My advice: before changing cities, settle your destination first. Set out only after you have a unit and a position; do not quit first and then go to try your luck. What suits you least is to start a business from zero somewhere else; you are good at taking over a stall that others have built and making it solid and big. If you have a family, try not to live apart in two places for the long term; if you really must be apart for a time, call on a fixed schedule every week and go home regularly, because family as a rear base is very important to you.

My advice: go out into the world with confidence. Studying, working and living long in other places are all stronger for you than staying at home. But while out there, there are a few things you must hold firm: go to nightlife venues less, stop drinking at seven-tenths, and do not stay late alone with an unfamiliar person of the opposite sex. In driving and outdoor activities, know your limits, and do not drive at night. When matters of signing, guarantees or cooperation with a grey area come up in another place, set them all aside first, then find someone who knows the field to look them over before you speak.

My advice: go out into the world with confidence. Studying, working and living long in other places are all stronger for you than staying where you are. While outside, set clear lines for your social life: go to nightlife venues less, do not drink much, and do not talk privately with a person of the opposite sex until late. Before you fall for someone, find out the other person's real circumstances: what the family situation is, what work they do and what the people around them say; ask about these things clearly before you invest your feelings. When driving far yourself and in outdoor activities, know your limits, and do not drive at night.

My advice: let yourself off a little. That others do not meet your standards does not mean they are wrong; with one less judgement, the people around you are relieved, and you are relieved too. When a task comes to you, first ask whether this is really your responsibility, and if not, do not take it on. When deciding you lean toward the steady side, which is fine, but every year or two force yourself to take on something you have never done. Do not lock yourself into one identity either; you can carry both the civil and the martial, and your road is wider than you think.

My advice: settle early on a home in your own name. In good times it is a help, and in hard times it is a backup card. Before large transactions, read the contract terms word by word once, and do not mind the trouble; for troubles with neighbours, the management office and decoration, spelling things out in advance takes less effort than arguing later.

My advice: talk with your child early about feelings and about the body. Also talk about proper limits when being around other people; do not avoid it, and the earlier you speak, the more natural it is. Support your child's artistic talent as best you can; suppressing it rigidly often brings emotional problems in return. When you are with your child, especially a son, give fewer orders and ask one more time what he thinks; set aside a stretch of time each week that belongs only to the two of you, and even just sharing a meal or playing a ball game works better than lecturing.

My advice: set the rules early, let go within the rules, and do not manage the details. When talking with your son, give fewer orders and lay out many facts so that he can choose for himself, and if he chooses wrongly, let him clean up the consequences himself. When children grow up they mostly go out into the world; whether studying or working they may be far away, and seeing each other little while being far apart is normal, so from childhood make the bond solid: call on a fixed schedule and remember what is going on in your child's life, and then distance will not stretch it.

My advice: seize early the opportunities for long-term business trips, study abroad or transfers between cities. Do not begrudge moving your place of residence. When you arrive somewhere new, actively cultivate two or three relationships in which you can talk from the heart, and do not live as a lonely island. When travelling far, buy an accident insurance plan, do not drive at night, do not play overly risky sports outdoors, and when walking alone at night, pay a little more attention. When Power is in effect, try to take a position of being in charge and sent out to another place.

My advice: seize early the opportunities for long-term business trips, study abroad or transfers between cities. Do not begrudge moving your place of residence. When you arrive somewhere new, actively cultivate two or three relationships in which you can talk from the heart, and do not live as a lonely island. When travelling far, buy an accident insurance plan, do not drive at night, do not play overly risky sports outdoors, and when walking alone at night, pay a little more attention. When Prosperity is in effect (money coming in), the road to money in other places will open up noticeably.

My advice: put up your boundaries early. Helping is fine, but say in advance which tasks you will not take on, and do not wait until the suppression turns into resentment before speaking. It is the same with your parents: going home regularly to eat, and going with them to their health check-ups, is far more practical than trying to persuade them to understand your way of life. For the things you do for this family, mention them offhandedly so that they know, and do not quietly finish them and leave it at that.

My advice: start a family a little later. Give each other more time to confirm; the old books say that with Strategist in the Spouse palace you should marry a wife who is younger and firmer in character, and that this actually suits you; this is for reference, not a hard condition. When living together, say directly what you think in your heart, and do not count on the other person to guess. When the two of you discuss things, set a rule: whoever comes up with an idea takes responsibility for the first step, so just do it first and work it out afterwards. In daily life arrange many small things to do together, such as cooking, going for walks or taking a trip; relying on conversation alone cannot support a relationship.

My advice: start a family a little later, because settling too early invites clashes. Put companionship into your schedule: each week set a fixed stretch of time that belongs only to her, with your phone put down; when you return from a business trip, first tell her about the people and things you met on the trip, and do not just report that you are safe. When she offers an opinion, do not treat it as nitpicking; it is mostly that she wants to be held in your heart. The fierce momentum of the early days together will fade, and the understanding that lets you live together has to be built up slowly.

My advice: marry a little later. The old books say that with Strategist in the Spouse palace the husband should be older than you; finding someone a little older makes living together smoother, but this is for reference, not a hard condition. When living together, if you are unsure in your heart, ask directly, and do not make up reasons in your head on the other person's behalf. Settle the division of work in advance: whoever raises a matter takes responsibility for the first step, so just do it first. Arrange many everyday tasks to do together, such as cooking, walking and taking a trip together; these hold a relationship steady far better than discussing the relationship again and again.

My suggestion: marry a little later, and decide once your state of mind is steady. Choose someone who is both tolerant of you and has views of their own: too soft and they cannot bear your weight, too hard and they will clash with you. Before marriage, lay out and compare your ways of living: who manages the money, whether you want children, whether you can accept that you go whenever you say you will go. These matter more than the feeling. Do not rush to remodel him either; say beforehand where you want change, and ask whether he is willing. In which decade and which year this Prosperity is triggered, you still need to check against the luck periods.

My advice: deliberately arrange a few “not so comfortable” things for your child. Sports teams, things that take long practice before they show results, and activities that require both cooperating with others and competing let your child taste early the link between effort and results. For what your child can do alone, do less on their behalf, and when they cannot manage it, do not rush to catch them at the bottom. If your child feels unwell, take them to a doctor and follow the doctor's advice; do not decide on your own.

My advice: consciously let your child be a child. Do not pour all the family's difficulties out to your child; digest your own emotions, and do not make your child your listener. When your child does not do well, allow it, and do not rush to lecture. Take your child to do a few useless things: playing ball, running around and staring into space are all fine. Physically, take your child for check-ups on schedule, and when unwell, listen to the doctor. The number of times you say thank you to your child works better than a hundred lectures.

My advice: if you have the means, before marriage buy yourself a small apartment as a backup card. This is not distrust of your other half, but you need a way of retreat that you can take at any time. When buying a home, do not expect to get it all in one step; give priority to a location and a type of apartment that is easy to resell, and treat “can be traded up later” as a hard criterion. Do not spend too much on decoration at one time; first live comfortably, and keep the rest for the next home.

My advice: each month, set aside a fixed budget for yourself. Use this sum for learning, fitness and your image. You are generous with others and too thrifty with yourself; this money looks like it is spent away, but in fact it buys back quality of life. For investing, you suit buying and holding, not frequent in and out, and you should not touch high-risk financial products. Arrange the couple's money as if playing one game of chess, and sit down once a year to go through the accounts together. Only when your marriage is stable will your wealth be stable.

My advice: each week leave a stretch of time that belongs entirely to you. Take no tasks and listen to no one's complaints; walking, staring into space or sitting in meditation are all fine. From middle age, try travelling alone, even for only three days, and you will find that the sky does not fall without you. When something weighs on your heart, do not push through it; find someone who can listen to you, or write it out. Do not treat worry as love: with many things you do not manage, they will turn out fine on their own.

My advice: each week leave a stretch of time that belongs entirely to you. Take no tasks and listen to no one's complaints; walking, staring into space or doing yoga are all fine. From middle age, try travelling alone, even for only three days, and you will find that the sky does not fall without you. When something weighs on your heart, do not push through it; find someone who understands you and talk. Do not treat worry as love: with many things you do not manage, they will turn out fine on their own.

My advice: each week set aside fixed time to be alone. Do not rush to look for something to do the moment you stop. When you meet misunderstanding and bad opinions, hold back for two days before responding; the more eager you are to repair things, the noisier the matter usually becomes. Decide important matters only after a night's sleep, and do not judge while your emotions are rising. Among friends, choose two or three who dare to tell you the truth to befriend deeply, and keep up the rest out of ordinary courtesy.

My suggestion: each week keep half a day just for yourself. Do nothing for anyone to see: painting, yoga or going alone to see an exhibition are all fine. Practise one sentence: “I don't feel like going today.” The first time you say it will feel awkward, and the second time it will come easily. After middle age, find a hobby that is not for money or for face, and arrange a trip alone. It is fine to be less polished now and then; the days are yours to live, not a performance for outsiders.

My advice: each week keep half a day entirely for yourself. Do not do it for anyone to see: writing a few lines, listening to music or walking a stretch of road alone are all fine. Practise one sentence: “I don't feel like going today.” The first time you say it will feel awkward, and the second time it will feel light. From middle age, find a hobby that is not for money or for face, and arrange a trip alone. Life is lived by you, not a performance for outsiders.

My advice: each day set aside a fixed stretch that uses only the body and not the mind. Walking, stretching, cooking or fixing small things are all fine, letting your attention settle in your hands. From middle age, choose one practice that gathers your focus into one place and keep it up long term: sitting meditation, tai chi, yoga or long-distance running are all fine, because reading and conversation alone cannot settle this restlessness of yours. Add one more rule: a matter that you have thought over for more than three days must be decided one way or the other, and if you choose wrongly, correct it as you go, and do not stay up all night in your head.

My advice: each day leave a stretch of time that does not count on any return. Even half an hour: a walk, yoga, tai chi, the kind of relaxation that gets the body moving works best for your restless nature. Make peace with your own instinct to earn money; there is no need to force yourself to take it lightly, just do not leave it switched on for twenty-four hours.

My advice: each day spend half an hour without using your mind. Meditation, yoga, light jogging, growing flowers or painting are all fine, letting your attention settle in your hands and body. Before sleeping, write down on paper the matters you have not finished thinking through, and when you have written them, close the notebook and tell yourself to work it out tomorrow. From middle age you can learn practices that gather your focus into one place, such as sitting meditation, and you can also find a professional counsellor to talk with; speaking what is in your heart is better than suppressing it yourself.

My advice: each day keep half an hour with no work and no meeting people. Even just a short walk will do, and once you are used to it, it will no longer feel uncomfortable. When tired, say so directly, and do not push until your body sounds the alarm. Put that stubborn streak into directions that are truly worth persisting in, and before you dig in, ask yourself one question: is this right, or do I just not want to admit defeat? What you need to learn is not to push harder, but to take back some of the light you shine outward and use it for yourself, so that what remains can shine for a long time.

My advice: every year, deliberately choose one thing that makes you uncomfortable. Changing position, taking on a project with uncertain results, or learning a craft that takes clumsy effort are all fine. Write a completion date for the goal, and then tell someone who will press you on it. Your foundation leans toward stability, and in the second half of life you mostly will not lack for a livelihood; what you really lack are the years before forty, and whether you manage to earn something for yourself in them.

My advice: have a health check-up once a year. Do not skip the eye examination; if your body feels unwell, see a doctor and follow the doctor's instructions. When your periods are heavy, pay attention to supplementing iron, eat with little salt and little oil, and cut down on alcohol if you can. During pregnancy, follow the rhythm of prenatal check-ups, and do not skip any because of work. Around the time before and after perimenopause, do not bear hot flashes, palpitations and poor sleep; see a doctor for an examination a few years early and adjust your routine. For exercise choose aerobic kinds such as brisk walking and swimming, and do not play sports with strong physical opposition.

My advice: have a health check-up once a year. Do not skip the eye examination, and after forty check more often; if your body feels unwell, see a doctor and follow the doctor's instructions, and do not push through it on your own. Eat with little salt and little oil, and cut down on alcohol if you can. For exercise choose aerobic kinds such as brisk walking, swimming and cycling, preferably outdoors, and do not go into matches with strong physical opposition. When your emotions rise, first leave the scene and walk for ten minutes, which works better than regretting it afterwards.

My advice: have a full health check-up once a year. While you are at it, answer an emotional questionnaire seriously; if something in your body is not right, see a doctor promptly and follow the doctor's advice, and do not bear it alone and then look it up online. Eat meals on time and go easy on very cold food. For exercise choose gentle kinds; yoga, tai chi and hiking are all fine, preferably with company, so that you speak out the words you have been suppressing as you move. There is one more thing that is the hardest and also the most effective: when you feel unwell, find someone to talk to, and allow others to help you.

My advice: have a full health check-up once a year. While you are at it, answer an emotional questionnaire seriously. When preparing for pregnancy, especially after thirty-five, see a specialist doctor early for an assessment and follow the doctor's advice, and do not flip through answers online on your own. Eat meals on time and go easy on very cold food. For exercise choose gentle kinds; yoga, tai chi and hiking are all fine, preferably with company. Most important is to nurture a small circle for yourself in which you can say what is in your heart, so that when you feel unwell someone will catch you.

My advice: have regular health check-ups every year.
